catalog_quote: [p. 408] Every word in classical Tibetan has a single primary STRESS that falls on the first syllable; bound forms (conjunctions, nominalizers, role particles, bound quantifiers) are thus considered unstressed, as are also ni and Yan, unless the latter is the first word of the proposition; free quantifiers, numerals, and determiners may also be unstressed in a weak position. We will symbolize a stressed syllable as 1 and an unstressed syllable as 0. (2) p.90, ch.6 sec.4 'Disyllabic Stress Groups' (djvu line 7285): '...for word…
new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per word, on the word-initial syllable; enclitic bound forms (case/role particles, nominalizers, conjunctions, ni, non-initial yang) are unstressed, so the typical Stem+Particle word is a trochee; words tend to be disyllabic stress groups with initial stress and reduction/omission of unstressed syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described; only a single primary stress per word is posited (p.90 says 'primary stress' on the first syllable of a disyllabic stress group, implying nothing further).
new_statements.exceptions: Bound forms and ni/yang unstressed unless yang is proposition-initial; free quantifiers, numerals and determiners may be unstressed in metrically weak position; in Old Tibetan bardic verse stress is 'neutralized' in the verse-final syllable (p.413). Note Jäschke 1883 sec.9.4 (p.13), describing spoken W./C. Tibetan reading, agrees on root-before-particle stress but puts compound accent on the latter member -- a partial contradiction.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the (phonological) word in a written classical language, made in the service of metrical analysis (strong/weak positions = stressed/unstressed syllables); Beyer's evidence is word-formation (disyllabic stress groups, clipping of unstressed syllables) and verse, not instrumental data. No tone is posited for Classical Tibetan (DeLancey 2003).
new_statements.identity_note: Beyer's statement is explicitly about 'classical Tibetan' (the written language, clas1254), with supporting diachronic remarks about Old Tibetan (Glottolog oldt1234? separate languoid) and modern dialects; Jäschke 1883's accent note is keyed to spoken Western/Central Tibetan reading pronunciation, and Hahn's pronunciation lesson to Lhasa reading pronunciation, not to Classical Tibetan as such.

sources.note: p.408 (ch.13 'Beyond the sentence', sec.5.1 Metrics: Definitions): 'Every word in classical Tibetan has a single primary STRESS that falls on the first syllable; bound forms... are thus considered unstressed'. p.90 (ch.6 Syllables, sec.4): words and common collocations form 'a single DISYLLABIC STRESS GROUP, usually with the primary stress on the first syllable'; unstressed syllables reduce/are omitted. p.413: in Old Tibetan bardic metre stress 'appears neutralized in the final syllable of each verse'.

sources.citation: Jäschke, H. A. 1883. Tibetan Grammar. 2nd ed., prepared by H. Wenzel. London: Trübner.
sources.note: sec.9.4, p.13: 'The accent is, in such cases, most naturally given to the root, or, in compounds, generally to the latter part of the composition, as: mig eye, míg-gi of the eye; lag hand, lag-šúb(s) glove' -- root stress before enclitic particles, but compound stress on the LATTER member (pronunciation notes keyed to spoken Western/Central Tibetan); partly contradicts Beyer.
